summary:
Same-sex relations are legal throughout Italy for men and women, and the age of consent is 14 regardless of gender or sexual orientation, a parity that predates the twentieth century. Cross-dressing is legal. The penal code of the 1920s–1940s banned it and police targeted transgender people during that period; a police officer was reportedly dismissed in 2006 for cross-dressing in public while off duty.

Italy has no single comprehensive law covering sexual orientation and gender identity; protection rests on court rulings and sectoral statutes. Sexual-orientation discrimination in employment has been illegal nationwide since July 2003 under Legislative Decree no. 216 of 2003, which implements EU Directive 2000/78/EC; Law no. 101 of 2008 removed the exemptions that had covered police, armed forces and rescue services. No other nationwide law covers sexual orientation or gender identity, and no Italian law explicitly bans transphobic discrimination, so transgender people may face discrimination in goods and services, housing, education and health care; ILGA-Europe's 2021 report notes the absence of nationwide protection for goods and services. A Rome court ruled on 15 January 2023 that firing a trans professor amounted to sex discrimination.

A bill banning homophobic and transphobic advertising in streets and on vehicles passed the Chamber of Deputies 271–16 on 28 October 2021 and the Senate 190–34 on 4 November, was signed by President Mattarella and took effect 10 November 2021; the government forced a single up-or-down vote on the whole bill, so MPs who opposed that provision had to vote for it. A broader anti-discrimination and hate-crime bill passed the Chamber 265–193 on 4 November 2020 but died in the Senate on 27 October 2021 by a 131–154 secret ballot.

Legal gender change has been possible since 1982, when Italy became the sixth country worldwide to allow it; since 21 May 2015 neither sterilisation nor sex reassignment surgery has been required. On 23 July 2024 the Constitutional Court, in judgment no. 143, first recognised non-binary individuals as rights-holders under Articles 2, 3 and 32 but declined to add a non-binary registry marker, holding that only Parliament can alter the male/female binary, and struck down the requirement of judicial authorisation for gender-affirming surgery after a legal sex change. Courts in Trento (15 February 2023) permitted legal gender change for transgender minors with parental consent and psychological consultation, and Trapani (6 July 2023) allowed a name and gender change with no surgery or hormones.

On 14 April 2025 the Supreme Court of Cassation ordered Italian identity cards to use the gender-neutral term "genitori" rather than "mother" and "father" for children with same-sex parents, finding the previous wording discriminatory. Citing the Constitutional Court's 2010 ruling that recognised same-sex couples as a "legitimate social formation," the Court of Cassation ordered a questura to grant a residence permit to an Algerian citizen married to a same-sex Spanish spouse. Italy recognises persecution based on sexual orientation or gender identity as grounds for asylum under the 1951 Geneva Convention and EU Qualification Directive 2011/95/EU, and Decree-Law No. 130/2020, in force 22 October 2020, simplified asylum procedures and reinforced protection for vulnerable groups including those persecuted on those grounds. Same-sex marriages performed abroad are registered as civil unions rather than marriages (Court of Cassation, May 2018).

Gay and bisexual men have been allowed to donate blood since 2001. Since February 2019 puberty blockers and cross-sex hormones have been provided free of charge under the National Health Service, and since 2020 hormone therapy has been fully covered. In 2018 the Italian National Bioethics Committee and the Italian Medicines Agency backed puberty blockers for adolescents with gender dysphoria case by case with safeguards; access still requires medical evaluation, parental consent and exhaustion of other interventions, a position supported by the Italian Society of Endocrinology, the Italian Academy of Pediatrics and six other paediatric and adolescent medical societies.

Regional statutes cover Tuscany (2004), Liguria (2009), Marche (2010), Sicily (2015), Piedmont (2016), Umbria (2017), Emilia-Romagna (2019), Campania (2020) and Apulia (2024).

Violence against transgender people continues. On 7 April 2026 an appeals court confirmed convictions for the assault of transgender tourists in Italy, affirming accountability for violence against trans visitors. On 5 July 2024 a Milan traffic officer was sentenced to 10 months for beating a transgender woman with a baton. ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2026, covering 2025, records that homophobic and transphobic violence continued, including organised dating-app entrapment schemes targeting gay men; in March 2025 the Civil Court of Asti recognised for the first time physical and psychological harm from homophobic mistreatment. The Education Ministry omitted LGBTI persecution from Holocaust Remembrance Day circulars for a second year, and a cardinal called homosexual acts 'a mortal sin'. HRW's World Report 2025 records political rhetoric hostile to LGBT people contributing to a hostile environment, alongside constraints on the rule of law and on civil society. Progetto Gionata reports that transphobia is the most atroce and diffuse discrimination facing transgender people in Italy.

In detention, a Ludwig Boltzmann Institute national report of July 2025 on LGBTIQ detainees in Italy documents homolesbobitransphobia and discrimination, pathways to gender affirmation, same-sex relationships, and the legal/policy framework for LGBTIQ people in Italian detention. A 2026 thematic analysis in Frontiers in Psychiatry of transgender identity and psychiatric care in Italian prisons records systemic gaps and institutional challenges for incarcerated trans people.

In May 2026 AGESCI, Italy's largest Catholic scout association, decided that sexual orientation and gender identity can no longer exclude adults from leadership and educational roles, after three years of internal debate. Pew found in 2013 that 86% of Italians aged 18–29 accepted homosexuality, against 67% of those over 50.
tangentialFactors: Outright International's country overview lists Italy's at-a-glance baseline as same-sex relations legal nationwide for men and women. Intrepid Travel presents Italy as an LGBTQIA+ destination for its travellers; the page carries no safety finding specific to Italy.
